overview.title: Graph mode vs XLA; starting a linear classifier in pure TensorFlow
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.subsection: 3.3.2 An end-to-end example: A linear classifier in pure TensorFlow
overview.main_topic: TensorFlow's two compilation modes (graph mode via @tf.function, XLA via jit_compile=True); the start of the end-to-end linear classifier: generating two linearly separable classes of 2D points with np.random.multivariate_normal
overview.central_idea: @tf.function runs a function in graph mode by default; adding jit_compile=True compiles it with XLA, which is often faster but costs more on the first call. With tensors, variables, operations and gradients in hand, you can build any gradient-descent model, starting here with synthetic data: 1,000 points per class drawn from 2D Gaussians with means [0, 3] and [3, 0] and a shared covariance [[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]].
overview.importance: It closes the TensorFlow basics and opens the first complete from-scratch training example of the chapter, which is later reimplemented in PyTorch (p.102) and JAX (p.112), making it the shared benchmark for comparing the frameworks.
learning_objectives: Distinguish graph mode from XLA compilation and enable each in code.
Explain the speed/first-call trade-off of XLA.
State why tensors, variables, operations and gradients are sufficient for gradient-descent models.
Read Listing 3.13 and explain what mean and covariance control in the generated point clouds.
prerequisites: Basic notions of mean and variance

summary:
**Two compilation modes** (completing p.92's sentence):

- **Graph mode**, the default: any function decorated with `@tf.function` runs in graph mode.
- **XLA** (Accelerated Linear Algebra), "a high-performance compiler for ML", enabled with `@tf.function(jit_compile=True)`, shown on the same `dense` function.

XLA often makes a function run faster than graph mode, but the first execution takes longer because the compiler has more work to do.

**3.3.2 An end-to-end example: a linear classifier in pure TensorFlow.** You now know tensors, variables, tensor operations and gradient computation, which is "enough to build any TensorFlow-based machine learning model based on gradient descent." The authors motivate the example as a classic interview task: implementing a linear classifier from scratch, which separates candidates with minimal ML background from those without.

**Synthetic data (Listing 3.13).** Two classes of "nicely linearly separable" points in the 2D plane, each with `num_samples_per_class = 1000` samples from `np.random.multivariate_normal`:

- negative samples: `mean=[0, 3]`,
- positive samples: `mean=[3, 0]`,
- both with `cov=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]`.

The callouts explain that the covariance matrix describes the **shape** of the point cloud and the mean its **position**; this covariance gives "an oval-like point cloud oriented from bottom left to top right." The two classes have different positions and the same shape. The next page stacks them into a `(2000, 2)` array and builds `(2000, 1)` targets (p.94).

concepts.name: Graph mode
concepts.definition: TensorFlow's default compilation mode, used by any @tf.function-decorated function.
concepts.intuition: Record the recipe once, then execute it efficiently.
concepts.technical: The function is traced into a graph that the TensorFlow runtime executes.
concepts.misconception: That graph mode and XLA are the same; XLA is a separate, opt-in mode.

concepts.name: XLA compilation
concepts.definition: Accelerated Linear Algebra, a high-performance compiler for ML, enabled with jit_compile=True.
concepts.intuition: A more thorough translator: slower to translate, faster result.
concepts.technical: @tf.function(jit_compile=True); often faster than graph mode with a costlier first call.
concepts.significance: A main source of TensorFlow's speed (p.98).
concepts.misconception: That XLA is always faster; the book says 'often'.

concepts.name: Linear classifier
concepts.definition: A model that assigns classes based on an affine function of the input.
concepts.intuition: Draw a straight line; points on one side are class 0, on the other class 1.
concepts.technical: Prediction = W·x + b, compared to a threshold; trained by gradient descent on a loss (in the following pages).
concepts.significance: The chapter's end-to-end example in all three frameworks.
concepts.example: Separating points around (0, 3) from points around (3, 0).
concepts.misconception: That it can separate any data; it needs (nearly) linearly separable classes.

concepts.name: Multivariate normal (mean and covariance)
concepts.definition: A Gaussian distribution over vectors, defined by a mean vector and a covariance matrix.
concepts.intuition: The callouts: the mean is the cloud's position, the covariance its shape.
concepts.technical: Off-diagonal 0.5 means the two coordinates are positively correlated (correlation 0.5 since variances are 1), tilting the cloud from bottom left to top right.
concepts.significance: Used to generate the two classes of Listing 3.13.
concepts.misconception: That cov=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]] has standard deviation 0.5; the diagonal entries are variances (1), the off-diagonal the covariance.

math.source_text: np.random.multivariate_normal(mean=[0, 3], cov=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]], size=num_samples_per_class); mean=[3, 0] for positive samples

variables.meaning: A 2D point from the negative / positive class
Shared covariance matrix: variances 1 on the diagonal, covariance 0.5 off the diagonal

math.operations: Independent sampling of 1,000 points per class.
math.purpose: Defines the synthetic dataset for the linear classifier.
math.interpretation: Both clouds have the same tilted oval shape; their centers are 3√2 ≈ 4.24 apart along the direction (1, −1), perpendicular to the tilt, so a straight line separates them well.
math.intuition: Two identical tilted ellipses placed on either side of the line y = x.
math.numerical_example: The correlation is 0.5/√(1·1) = 0.5. The midpoint of the means is (1.5, 1.5), which lies on y = x; by symmetry the line y = x is a natural decision boundary (our observation, not the book's).

code.title: Generating two classes of random points in a 2D plane
code.original_code:
import numpy as np

num_samples_per_class = 1000
negative_samples = np.random.multivariate_normal(
    mean=[0, 3], cov=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]], size=num_samples_per_class
)
positive_samples = np.random.multivariate_normal(
    mean=[3, 0], cov=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]], size=num_samples_per_class
)
code.what_it_does: Generates 1,000 random 2D points for each of two classes, from Gaussians with different means and the same covariance.

Other class: different mean, same covariance, i.e. different position, same shape.

deeper.title: Reading a covariance matrix
deeper.body:
For $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.5\\0.5 & 1\end{pmatrix}$:

- Diagonal entries are the variances of each coordinate (1 → standard deviation 1).
- The off-diagonal 0.5 is the covariance: when x is above its mean, y tends to be too. That positive correlation is why the callout calls the cloud "oriented from bottom left to top right."
- Its eigenvectors are $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ (eigenvalue 1.5, long axis) and $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$ (eigenvalue 0.5, short axis).

The class means differ by $(3, -3)$, i.e. along the **short** axis, where each cloud has standard deviation only $\sqrt{0.5} \approx 0.71$; the separation along that axis is about $4.24 / 0.71 \approx 6$ standard deviations, which is why the classes are "nicely" separable. (Analysis beyond the book.)

deeper.title: Graph mode vs XLA: when to pick which
deeper.body: Start eagerly to debug (p.92), then add `@tf.function` (graph mode). If the function is hot (called thousands of times) try `jit_compile=True` and time it: the book says XLA is *often* faster but has a costlier first run. This decision procedure is our inference from the text.

takeaways: TensorFlow has two compilation modes: graph mode (@tf.function) and XLA (@tf.function(jit_compile=True)).
XLA is often faster than graph mode but slower on the first call.
Tensors, variables, ops and gradients suffice for any gradient-descent model.
The end-to-end example is a linear classifier on two Gaussian clouds of 1,000 points each.
Mean sets a cloud's position, covariance its shape; both classes share cov=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]].

questions.question: How do you enable XLA compilation for a TensorFlow function?
questions.explanation: Shown on the page. Plain @tf.function gives graph mode; @tf.xla is not the API; run_functions_eagerly disables compilation.

questions.question: What does XLA stand for, and what trade-off does it have versus graph mode?
questions.answer: Accelerated Linear Algebra; often faster than graph mode, but the first execution takes longer because the compiler does more work.

questions.question: According to the callouts, what do the mean and the covariance matrix describe about each point cloud?
questions.answer: The mean describes its position in the plane; the covariance matrix describes its shape.
questions.explanation: The two classes have different positions (means) and the same shape (covariance).

questions.question: What shape does negative_samples have?
questions.explanation: 1,000 samples of 2D points (confirmed on p.94). (2000, 2) is the stacked array built next; the others transpose or drop an axis.

questions.question: What is the Euclidean distance between the two class means, and what is the correlation between the two coordinates within a class?
questions.explanation: Means (0, 3) and (3, 0); covariance 0.5 with unit variances.

questions.question: Why is this dataset well suited to a linear classifier?
questions.answer: It is designed to be linearly separable: two compact clouds with the same shape, centered far apart, so a straight line divides them.
questions.explanation: The authors call it 'nicely linearly separable synthetic data'.

questions.question: Can you list the ingredients you'll need from 3.3.1 to train this classifier, and which TensorFlow API provides each?
questions.answer: Parameters W and b as tf.Variable; forward pass and loss with ops like tf.matmul; gradients with tf.GradientTape; updates with assign_sub; optionally speed with @tf.function.
questions.explanation: These are exactly the pieces the page says suffice for any gradient-descent model.
